beats.intro: Chapter six, lesson four. Lysosomes, vacuoles, and the endomembrane system. [[chase]]Under a microscope, a white blood cell chases a bacterium. [[catch]]It catches it, swallows it whole, and destroys it. [[ask]]What does a cell use to digest something, and where does the digestion happen?
beats.tour: Here is our tour map of the cell. [[lit]]Today we visit the lysosomes, and the vacuoles. [[dim]]Everything else is dimmed, because lessons two and three covered the nucleus, the ribosomes, the {{ER|E R}}, and the Golgi. [[push]]Let's push in on a lysosome.
beats.lyso: A lysosome is a membranous sac of hydrolytic enzymes that digest macromolecules. [[sac]]The sac keeps the enzymes shut inside, away from the rest of the cell. [[hyd]]Hydrolytic means they break bonds using water, the reverse of building a polymer. [[four]]Lysosomal enzymes can break down proteins, fats, polysaccharides, and nucleic acids. [[why]]Keeping them in a sac matters. Loose in the cytoplasm, they would digest the cell itself.
beats.phago: Back to the white blood cell. This is phagocytosis. [[one]]Step one. The cell engulfs a particle, wrapping its plasma membrane around it. [[two]]Step two. The particle ends up inside a vesicle called a food vacuole. [[three]]Step three. A lysosome fuses with the food vacuole. [[four]]Step four. The enzymes spill in and digest the contents. The lysosome does not turn into the vacuole. It fuses with it. [[small]]The small molecules that result can then be used by the cell.
beats.q1: Quick check. Put the steps of phagocytosis in order.
beats.auto: Lysosomes also clean up from the inside. [[old]]Cells have old or damaged organelles, like a worn out mitochondrion, or a peroxisome. [[wrap]]A membrane wraps around them, forming a vesicle. [[fuse]]A lysosome fuses with that vesicle, [[dig]]and its enzymes digest the organelles into parts the cell can reuse. [[name]]This recycling is called autophagy. The cell eats its own worn out parts, and gets building blocks back.
beats.vacuole: Now vacuoles. A vacuole is a membrane bound compartment, and there are several kinds. [[food]]Food vacuoles form by phagocytosis, as we just saw. [[contr]]Contractile vacuoles are found in many freshwater protists. A pond cell takes in water all the time, so the vacuole collects the excess and pumps it out of the cell. [[central]]Central vacuoles are found in many mature plant cells. They hold water and organic compounds. [[some]]A plant or fungal cell may have one or several vacuoles, but other cells have them too.
beats.central: Look closer at a plant cell. [[leaf]]A crisp lettuce leaf is crisp because its cells are full of water. [[big]]The central vacuole fills most of the cell, and pushes the cytosol out into a thin layer against the cell wall. [[wilt]]Without water, the vacuole shrinks, and the leaf goes limp. [[where]]The nucleus, and the chloroplasts, sit in that thin layer of cytosol.
beats.q2: Quick check. Match each vacuole to its job.
beats.route: Now let's tie this lesson to the last one. Many membranes in the cell work as one connected system, the endomembrane system. [[er]]Start at the nucleus. Its envelope is joined to the endoplasmic reticulum, and the rough {{ER|E R}}, studded with ribosomes, builds proteins. Smooth {{ER|E R}} has no ribosomes. [[ves]]Transport vesicles bud off the {{ER|E R}}, and carry their cargo along. [[cis]]They fuse with the cis face of the Golgi, the side that receives. [[mod]]The Golgi modifies, sorts, and packs the products. [[trans]]They leave from the trans face, the side that ships. [[lyso]]Some vesicles become lysosomes, which stay in the cell. [[pm]]Others travel to the plasma membrane, and fuse with it, releasing their contents outside the cell. That is exocytosis.
beats.example: Let's follow two proteins from the same Golgi. [[a]]The first is a digestive enzyme. [[a2]]It is made on the rough {{ER|E R}}, passes through the Golgi, and leaves in a vesicle that becomes a lysosome. [[b]]The second is a protein a cell sends out, such as insulin. [[b2]]It follows the same road, but its vesicle goes to the plasma membrane, and releases it outside. [[same]]Same factory, same shipping dock. The sorting at the trans face decides the destination.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Lysosomes are sacs of hydrolytic enzymes that digest proteins, fats, polysaccharides, and nucleic acids. [[w2]]In phagocytosis, a lysosome fuses with a food vacuole. In autophagy, it recycles old organelles. [[w3]]Vacuoles come in kinds. Food, contractile, and central. [[w4]]And the endomembrane route runs from {{ER|E R}}, to vesicle, to Golgi, to a lysosome or the plasma membrane. [[end]]Now try the practice.
